strapline: Botswana answers for Khama; a minister's warning before 25 November; education's 13.4%; a survival plan at Zambia Railways; and the under-15s at State House

stories.title: 'Excellent diplomatic relations': Botswana's foreign minister distances his government from Ian Khama's attack on Hichilema, as Khama says he will not apologise
stories.excerpt: Dr Phenyo Butale, Botswana's Minister of International Relations, has said that the former president's description of Hakainde Hichilema as 'Africa's newest dictator' is not his government's position, and has defended Gaborone's attendance at the September inauguration, The Zambian Observer reported on Sunday 8 November. Mr Khama told the Botswana Gazette last week that he stands by his allegations. Neither report records a formal exchange between the two governments.

image.label: Gaborone and Lusaka
image.caption: Botswana's foreign minister says a former president's criticism of President Hichilema does not speak for the government in Gaborone.

body: Botswana's government has drawn a line between itself and its former president. Dr Phenyo Butale, the Minister of International Relations, has said that Ian Khama's description of President Hakainde Hichilema as "Africa's newest dictator" does not reflect official policy, and has defended the decision to attend Mr Hichilema's inauguration after the August general election, The Zambian Observer reported on Sunday 8 November. The Observer said the minister spoke in a telephone interview and to Botswana's The Voice newspaper; it did not say on which day.

body.text: We enjoy excellent diplomatic relations with Zambia, hence we attended the inauguration of President Hichilema.
body.attribution: Dr Phenyo Butale, Botswana's Minister of International Relations, in a telephone interview quoted by The Zambian Observer on Sunday 8 November

body: The minister's case, as the Observer set it out, is about who speaks for a state. The opinions of an individual, he said, "should not be taken as representative of the policy or position of the sitting Government", whatever office that individual once held. Remarks by a former head of state can be mistaken for an official line, he said, and the government was alive to the possibility that this could affect "diplomatic confidence, complicate bilateral engagement" and damage Botswana's standing abroad. He added that Botswana had held no discussions with Zambia about the outcome of its election and that foreign policy is communicated through authorised government institutions. He did not dispute Mr Khama's right to speak: the Observer reported that he defended the former president's constitutional freedom to express an opinion while urging former officials to act responsibly on sensitive international matters.

The remark that started it was made in Ntlo ya Dikgosi in Gaborone, where Mr Khama sits as Kgosi Khama IV, while he was questioning Dr Butale about Botswana's attendance at the inauguration, the Botswana Gazette reported on 4 November. The same paper had reported on 28 October that he used the chamber to challenge the UDC government over what the paper described as its reluctance to condemn alleged abuses in other African states, naming Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda and Zambia, and that Dr Butale replied that Botswana works through regional and continental bodies and observes the principle of non-interference. President Duma Boko attended Mr Hichilema's second-term inauguration in Lusaka on 1 September, the Gazette reported on 30 September.

Mr Khama has not retreated. "Absolutely, I will not apologise," he told the Gazette in the report published on 4 November, in which he stood by allegations of political persecution and interference with electoral and judicial processes in Zambia, cited arrests, detentions and beatings, and said Zambians had sent him messages of thanks. In September he had told the same paper that his public criticism did not run parallel to Botswana's foreign policy and that no minister had called him to object.

The Zambian response has come from several directions. The Gazette quoted State House Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka as saying Zambians "can't believe those statements are attributed to a former President", reported that former Vice-President Enock Kavindele had urged Mr Khama to respect Zambia's sovereignty and produce evidence, and quoted nominated MP Judith Kabemba Nkonge calling the remarks "reckless and unbecoming of a former head of state". A youth advocate, Mukuka Kampamba, demanded a public apology within 24 hours and asked President Boko to step in, the paper said. UPND Deputy Secretary General Gertrude Imenda told News Diggers that Mr Khama should concentrate on his own country's affairs and that the Patriotic Front had been more dictatorial in office than the UPND, the paper reported on 7 November.

Not every Zambian voice has been critical of the former president. Tonse Alliance chairman Sakwiba Sikota said on Monday 2 November that the description reflected growing concern about democracy and human rights in Zambia, according to the same News Diggers report. Human Rights Watch said on 2 November that it had documented 14 apparent enforced disappearances in August and 71 arrests on charges it considered potentially politically motivated, Zambia Monitor reported; the Gazette notes that Mr Hichilema's government rejects allegations of electoral wrongdoing.

What Dr Butale's statement settles is narrow. He has said that Mr Khama's words are not Botswana's; he has not, in the remarks reported, said whether they are true. None of the reports read for this edition records a formal protest from Lusaka to Gaborone, a reply from Zambia's foreign ministry to the minister's remarks, or any step by Botswana's government to restrain the former president.

body.title: The sequence, as reported
items: 1 September: President Duma Boko attends Mr Hichilema's second-term inauguration in Lusaka (Botswana Gazette)
30 September: Mr Khama says no minister has asked him to stop criticising African leaders (Botswana Gazette)
28 October: the Gazette reports his challenge in Ntlo ya Dikgosi over Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda and Zambia; Dr Butale cites non-interference
4 November: "Absolutely, I will not apologise" (Botswana Gazette)
8 November: The Zambian Observer reports Dr Butale's statement that the remarks are not government policy

body.confirmed: Dr Butale is reported by The Zambian Observer to have said that Mr Khama's views are not Botswana's policy and that Botswana attended the inauguration because of its relations with Zambia. Mr Khama told the Botswana Gazette he will not apologise. State House, a former Vice-President, a nominated MP and the UPND's deputy secretary general have criticised his remarks, according to the Gazette and News Diggers.
body.unverified: Mr Khama's allegations of persecution and electoral interference are his own and are rejected by the Zambian government. The Observer does not say when Dr Butale spoke, and its account has not been checked against The Voice's original report. Whether the two governments have communicated formally about the matter has not been reported.

stories.title: Andeleki warns that Zambia is no banana republic, a governance group calls the 25 November march 'shooting in the air', and a UPND official says the term-limit debate should go on
stories.excerpt: Dr Clement Andeleki said at a ministerial handover that the government would not tolerate anyone trying to throw Zambia into disarray and warned church leaders and politicians to stay within their mandate, News Diggers reported on Sunday 8 November. The paper set the remarks beside civil society's notice to the police of a march in defence of the two-term limit. Opinion on the march, and on the debate itself, is divided, including inside the ruling party.

image.label: Before 25 November
image.caption: The Home Affairs minister has warned against attempts to cause disorder, ahead of a civil society march over presidential term limits planned for 25 November.

body: The Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security, Dr Clement Andeleki, has said the government will not tolerate anyone who tries to throw the country into disarray, and that Zambia is not a banana republic, News Diggers reported on Sunday 8 November. Speaking at a ministerial handover ceremony, he said the government had taken note of people agitating to cause chaos and gave an assurance that they would not succeed, the paper said. He also warned church leaders and politicians against operating outside their mandate.

News Diggers placed the warning beside a second fact: a consortium of civil society organisations has notified the Zambia Police Service of a peaceful procession planned for 25 November against calls to remove presidential term limits. The part of the report that was open to non-subscribers does not show the minister naming the march or its organisers, and it does not give the date or place of the ceremony. The connection between the two is the paper's, not, on the evidence available, the minister's.

A separate News Diggers report on the same day showed how divided opinion outside government is. Luckson Lungu, board chairperson of the GEARS Initiative, a governance group, described the organisations planning the march as "shooting in the air". Governance activist Wisdom Muyunda took the opposite line on the substance, urging Members of Parliament to drop calls to lift the limit and saying the argument risks diverting the country from its economic priorities. The paper named the organisers as Chapter One Foundation, Transparency International Zambia, LCK Foundation and ActionAid, and recalled that a group of youths had earlier marched to Parliament to hand in a petition in favour of removal.

The ruling party is not speaking with one voice either. Gertrude Imenda, the UPND's deputy secretary general and an MP, said that because there are people on both sides the debate should continue, and that she has a position of her own which she is keeping to herself, Daily Revelation reported in its Monday 9 November edition under a headline quoting her as saying she had kept it "in my heart". Three days earlier The Zambian Observer reported UPND media director Mark Simuuwe as saying that most Zambians agree the limit should go and that only a few people, whom he associated with the opposition, object. The Observer noted that he cited no poll or survey for the claim.

body.text: Two terms are enough. Democracy must prevail. Our constitutional safeguards must remain intact.
body.attribution: Dr Brian Mushimba, president of the Organized People's Party, in a statement carried by The Zambian Observer on 4 November

body: The visible part of the News Diggers report says that the government, through Chief Government Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu, had urged the organisers on the matter, but the sentence is cut off by the paper's paywall. What the reports read for this edition do not show is whether the police have replied to the notification, whether any conditions have been attached to it, and whom the minister had in mind when he spoke of church leaders acting outside their mandate.

body.confirmed: Dr Andeleki made the remarks at a ministerial handover ceremony, according to News Diggers. Civil society groups have notified the police of a procession on 25 November, the same paper reports. GEARS has criticised the march; Ms Imenda and Mr Simuuwe of the UPND have made the statements attributed to them by Daily Revelation and The Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: Whether the minister's warning was aimed at the march is not established: the full text of his remarks was behind a paywall. Mr Simuuwe's claim that a majority of Zambians support removing term limits is unsupported by any published survey. The police response to the notification has not been reported.

stories.title: K38.24 billion and still short of a fifth: a teachers' union says education's 13.4% of the 2027 budget is not enough, as News Diggers asks whether pupils are learning
stories.excerpt: The National Union of Public and Private Educators of Zambia welcomed the rise in the education allocation from K33.04 billion to K38.24 billion but said its 13.4% share of the K284.8 billion budget falls below the 20% international benchmark, News Diggers reported on Sunday 8 November. On the published figures, debt service will take K67.6 billion. School feeding is to rise from K523 million to K1 billion.

image.label: 13.4% for education
image.caption: Education is allocated K38.24 billion in the 2027 budget, which a teachers' union says is below the 20% share it wants the government to aim for.

body: A complaint about the spending side of the 2027 budget has come from the classroom. The National Union of Public and Private Educators of Zambia (NUPPEZ) said in a statement on Saturday 7 November that the 13.4% of the budget going to education is below the 20% it described as the internationally recognised threshold, News Diggers reported on Sunday 8 November. The union's executive president, Charity Kampamba, began by welcoming the increase: Finance Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane proposed K38.24 billion for the sector on Friday 6 November, up from K33.04 billion in the 2026 budget.

The arithmetic is straightforward. K38.24 billion is 13.4% of the K284.8 billion total, and the rise on last year is K5.2 billion, a little under 16%. A fifth of the 2027 budget would be about K57 billion, so the distance between the allocation and the union's benchmark is in the region of K18.7 billion. Those last three figures are this desk's calculations from the published numbers, not the union's.

News Diggers took up the theme in its editorial on Monday 9 November, under the headline "Govt must make K38.2bn count in classrooms". Free education has brought millions of children through the school gate, the paper wrote, and the question now is whether they are learning. It reported that Ms Kampamba had said the allocation was insufficient for the sector's growing demands and that the union had questioned the absence of a provision it expected to see; the paper's account of that point is behind its paywall.

body.text: What else the education line sits beside

body: Other readings of the same budget help place the number. Education and health together receive K68.5 billion, about 24% of proposed spending, and funding for school feeding nearly doubles from K523 million to K1 billion, according to economist Lubinda Haabazoka's analysis as reported by Zambia Monitor on 7 November. He argued that the feeding money could ease the burden on families and give local farmers who supply schools a reliable market. Health's share is K30.3 billion, according to an analysis by The People's Brief published in The Zambian Observer on Sunday 8 November.

The same analysis gives the comparison that frames the union's complaint: debt service is put at K67.6 billion, about 23.7% of the budget, which is nearly as much as education and health together and about K29 billion more than education alone. Domestic revenue is expected to cover K233.7 billion, or 82.1% of the total, up from 58.7% in 2021, it said. The government's argument, in the minister's words quoted there, is that "there are no donors to pay, we must pay ourselves".

Neither the union's statement as reported nor the editorial sets out how a 20% share would be financed, and none of the reports read for this edition records a reply from the Ministry of Finance or the Ministry of Education. The People's Brief argued that Parliament should scrutinise the proposals before they take effect on 1 January 2027.

body.title: The education number in context

Education, 2026: K33.04 billion (News Diggers)
NUPPEZ benchmark: 20% of the budget, about K57 billion on the 2027 total (calculation)
Health, 2027: K30.3 billion (The Zambian Observer); education and health together K68.5 billion (Zambia Monitor)
School feeding: K523 million to K1 billion (Zambia Monitor)
Debt service: K67.6 billion, about 23.7% (The Zambian Observer)

stories.title: Three hundred jobs out of 688, and October's pay late: Daily Revelation reports a survival plan at Zambia Railways, and Kalaba asks what it says about the growth agenda
stories.excerpt: The state-owned railway's board and management have not answered reports that they proposed laying off 300 of 688 workers, Daily Revelation reports, and a staff memo dated 26 October said October salaries were delayed because operational problems had hit cash flow. Board chairperson Emmanuel Hachipuka has said jobs will have to go for the company to survive. The job-loss figure rests on one newspaper and has not been confirmed by the company.

image.label: Zambia Railways
image.caption: Daily Revelation reports that Zambia Railways has proposed cutting 300 of its 688 jobs under a survival plan; the company has not confirmed the figure.

body: Zambia Railways Limited, the state-owned operator, is reported to be planning to shed more than four in ten of its workers. Daily Revelation reports that the company's board and management have not responded to reports that they proposed laying off 300 workers out of 688 as part of a survival plan, and in its Monday 9 November edition the paper carries Citizens First leader Harry Kalaba's criticism of the government's silence on the matter. The figure comes from that one newspaper. No statement from the company, the Industrial Development Corporation or the government confirming or denying it was found for this edition.

What the company's own chairperson has said, according to the paper, points the same way. Emmanuel Hachipuka told Daily Revelation in a recent interview that "some people will have to lose their jobs in order for the company to survive", and the paper has separately reported him as saying the company had been asked to come up with a survival plan in which jobs would be lost. In an editorial in its 19 October edition the paper reported his account that the railway was spending 71 ngwee of every kwacha it earned on wages, against what he called an industry norm of 30 ngwee, and was already struggling to pay staff when its former managing director, Cuthbert Malindi, left.

body.text: Late salaries and a row over the board

body: The cash problem is documented in the company's own words. A memo to staff from the director of human resource and administration, Clyde Muleya, dated 26 October 2026, said that operational challenges had negatively affected cash flow and that October salaries had therefore been delayed, Daily Revelation reported. The same paper has reported that employees have asked, through the state's Industrial Development Corporation, for Mr Hachipuka's board to be dissolved, alleging interference in day-to-day operations and raising questions about appointments and the use of company resources. Mr Hachipuka called the allegations unfair and has said he will wait for the authorities to respond, the paper reported.

Mr Kalaba's argument is political. He said the government's silence over the planned job cuts shows that the UPND administration's description of the President's final term as a growth agenda is empty, Daily Revelation reported, and the paper's headline asks whether the railway is being allowed to decline to the advantage of private operators ahead of the planned repeal of the Railways Act. That is a question, not a finding: no evidence for it is set out in the part of the report open to non-subscribers, and no government response to it has been reported.

body.text: The plan the railway had in March

body: Earlier reporting by other outlets shows how far the company is from where it meant to be. In March, Zambia Railways appointed Pangaea Securities to help it raise US$60 million from development finance institutions and private investors, to sit alongside a €50 million European Union grant for track, signalling and communications, Zambia Monitor reported on 19 March and Railway Gazette International on 1 April. Its 2024–2028 business plan aimed to lift freight from 800,000 tonnes in 2024 to 2.6 million tonnes by 2028, with a first phase costed at US$113 million. Mr Malindi, then managing director, compared the railway to "a stool with three broken legs": rolling stock, track and operational efficiency, all of which he said had to be mended at once.

Whether the US$60 million has been raised, how many jobs the survival plan would actually remove, on what terms, and whether the October salaries have since been paid are not answered in any of the reports read for this edition.

body.confirmed: Daily Revelation reports that a company memo dated 26 October said October salaries were delayed, and quotes the board chairperson as saying jobs must be lost for the company to survive. Zambia Monitor and Railway Gazette International reported in March and April that the railway was seeking US$60 million alongside a €50 million EU grant.
body.unverified: The figure of 300 job losses out of 688 is reported by Daily Revelation alone and has not been confirmed by Zambia Railways, the IDC or the government. The suggestion that the company is being allowed to deteriorate to favour private operators is a question raised in a headline, not an established fact. The employees' allegations against the board are disputed by its chairperson.

stories.title: Up six places to 15th: the 2026 Ibrahim Index puts Zambia among Africa's ten most improved on governance, on data that stop before the August election
stories.excerpt: Zambia scored 58.4 out of 100 in the Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index, a gain of 5.1 points over 2016–2025 that lifted it from 21st to 15th of 54 countries, Zambia Monitor and the Daily Nation reported last week. Citizen participation rose more than anywhere else in Africa. Satisfaction with infrastructure fell by 30.4 points. The period measured ends in 2025, before the disputed aftermath of this year's vote.

image.label: Ibrahim Index 2026
image.caption: Zambia rose from 21st to 15th of 54 countries in the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance, which measures the decade to 2025.

body: Zambia has climbed six places in the continent's best-known governance ranking. The 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance, which the Mo Ibrahim Foundation launched on 31 October, places the country 15th of 54, up from 21st, with a score of 58.4 out of 100, Zambia Monitor reported on 5 November and the Daily Nation on 6 November. The score is 5.1 points higher than in 2016, which puts Zambia among the ten most improved countries in Africa over the decade the index covers.

Most of the gain is recent. Zambia Monitor reported that the pace of improvement quickened after 2021, with the overall score rising 6.4 points from that year, which on those figures means it had slipped slightly in the years before. The Daily Nation's summary made the same point, saying progress accelerated from 2021.

The largest single movement was in citizen participation, up 15.5 points since 2016, the biggest rise recorded by any African country, according to Zambia Monitor, which said the index found the improvement "particularly evident following the August 2021 general election". The rights measure rose 9.5 points. On the indicator the index calls Absence of Civil Society Repression Zambia moved from 29th to 10th, and on Rights and Civil Liberties for Women it is ranked first on the continent.

Two economic measures also moved sharply. Rural market access improved by 45.3 points, the largest gain in Africa, and access to mobile money accounts by 47.5 points, Zambia Monitor reported. One indicator went the other way: citizens' satisfaction with infrastructure fell by 30.4 points over the period.

body.text: What the index does not yet measure

body: The dates matter for how the ranking is read at home. The improvement is measured over 2016 to 2025, so the index does not take in the general election of 13 August 2026 or what has followed it. Human Rights Watch said on 2 November that it had documented 14 apparent enforced disappearances in August, 61 cases of beatings or other violence during arrest or detention, and 71 arrests on charges it regarded as potentially politically motivated, Zambia Monitor reported. Eighteen people have been charged with treason, the same report said. The police have given their own account of the most serious incident, the raid of 14 August on opposition leader Brian Mundubile's Lusaka home, in which opposition members allege that former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed by security forces: the Inspector General has said officers came under gunfire and returned fire.

Both things can be true: a decade's data showing wider participation and stronger rights scores, and a set of allegations from the past three months that the next edition of the index will have to weigh. Neither report recorded a government or opposition comment on the ranking, and neither gave the scores of other countries for comparison.

Citizen participation: +15.5 points, the largest gain in Africa
Rights: +9.5 points; Absence of Civil Society Repression: 29th to 10th
Rights and Civil Liberties for Women: 1st in Africa

stories.title: 150 Special Forces personnel and a clean-up in Kamwala: the unit marks its anniversary with the mayor's campaign on Monday, and two opposition leaders say it is the council's job
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Special Forces are to provide 150 personnel on Monday 9 November to clean the stretch between the Universal Church and the FINDECO flyover, The Zambian Observer reports, as part of the unit's annual day. Mayor Chitambala Mwewa welcomed the help. Socialist Party president Fred M'membe and Democratic Union president Ackim Njobvu have objected to elite soldiers doing municipal work. The deployment is reported by one outlet.

image.label: Kamwala, Monday
image.caption: The Special Forces are reported to be sending 150 personnel to clean part of Kamwala in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, the unit's annual day.

body: Lusaka's clean-up campaign is due to get an unusual workforce on Monday 9 November. The Zambia Special Forces will provide 150 personnel to clean the area between the Universal Church and the FINDECO flyover bridge in Kamwala, The Zambian Observer reported on 6 November in an account credited to Zambian Watch. The unit's commander, Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya, announced the exercise during a courtesy call on the Mayor of Lusaka, Chitambala Mwewa, the report said. No second outlet's account of the announcement was found for this edition, and whether the exercise has gone ahead was not known at the time of writing.

The explanation given is the calendar. The unit marks Special Forces Day every year on 9 November, and this year's observance is built around cleanliness, the Observer reported, under the theme "43 Years of Elite Service: Defending the Nation, Serving the Community." General Shapwaya said the exercise was meant to support the mayor's efforts. Mr Mwewa thanked the unit, said its help would speed up the work and reinforce the campaign against disorder in the city, and said the council was ready to work with it on what he calls the Make Lusaka Clean agenda. He added that the offer showed most residents were happy with the council's efforts, according to the report.

Two opposition leaders have criticised the plan. Ackim Njobvu, president of the Democratic Union, said highly trained soldiers should not be given work other institutions could do, and suggested the Zambia National Service or correctional facilities instead, the Observer reported on 6 November.

body.text: Our country is losing direction. We are abusing our men in uniform. They deserve RESPECT.
body.attribution: Ackim Njobvu, president of the Democratic Union, in remarks carried by The Zambian Observer on 6 November

body: The Socialist Party went further in a statement signed by its president, Fred M'membe, and published by the same outlet on 7 November. The party said it fully supports the goal of a clean and orderly capital, but questioned the use of specialised combat units for routine sanitation, calling it an institutional overstep that undermines civilian governance. "A clean Lusaka cannot be sustained through sporadic military interventions or public relations exercises," the statement said. If the council cannot keep the city clean, it argued, that is a failure of local government funding and administration, and the answer is to resource the council properly and pay its workers fairly.

The exercise is the latest turn in a drive that began soon after Mr Mwewa's election. Zambia Monitor reported on 23 August that the new mayor had launched a campaign called "Throw It in the Bin" and was touring the city with a loudhailer urging residents, traders and motorists to stop littering, and on 12 September that the removal of street vendors from parts of the city had begun, with the council expected to keep moving traders to designated markets. Both reports recorded strong approval on social media.

What separates the two positions is not whether Kamwala should be clean. The mayor and the commander present a one-day anniversary gesture of community service; the critics see a precedent for using the military in civil administration. The reports do not say who is meeting the cost of the exercise, whether council workers are taking part alongside the soldiers, or whether the Ministry of Defence approved it. The Observer recorded no reply from the council or the government to the criticism.

body.confirmed: The Socialist Party and the Democratic Union have publicly criticised a plan to use Special Forces personnel in a Lusaka clean-up; their statements were published by The Zambian Observer. The mayor's clean-up and vendor-removal campaigns since August are reported by Zambia Monitor.
body.unverified: The details of the deployment, including the number of personnel, the area and the date, come from one outlet, The Zambian Observer, crediting Zambian Watch. Whether the exercise took place as announced on Monday 9 November was not known when this edition was compiled.

stories.title: 'I will invite all mining firms': Hichilema hosts the under-15 champions at State House and promises to help FAZ clear a legacy debt whose size is reported two ways
stories.excerpt: The President told the squad that won Tier B of the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku that he would convene the mining houses to raise money for the Football Association of Zambia and help dismantle its old debt, on condition that it stops living beyond its means, ZamFoot reported on Sunday 8 November. FAZ president Keith Mweemba put the debt at not less than K40 million; the same report elsewhere says more than K140 million.

image.label: Champions at State House
image.caption: President Hichilema received the under-15 side that won Tier B of the FIFA U-15 World Cup and promised to help the FA with its legacy debt.

body: The boys who won in Baku have had their reception, and the Football Association of Zambia has come away from it with a presidential promise. President Hakainde Hichilema hosted the men's under-15 national team at State House after their victory in Tier B of the FIFA U-15 World Cup, where they beat Portugal 5–2 in the final under coach Brian Kunsanama, and told the association he would bring the mining companies together to raise money for it, ZamFoot reported on Sunday 8 November in an account credited to FAZ Media. Daily Revelation's Monday edition, describing the same meet-and-greet ceremony, places it a day before publication, on Sunday.

body.text: I will invite all mining firms to a meeting to help raise funds for FAZ.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, at the State House reception for the under-15 national team, as reported by ZamFoot on Sunday 8 November

body: The promise answered a request. FAZ president Keith Mweemba used his speech to raise what he called one of the association's lingering headaches, its legacy debt, reminding the President that the matter had first been put to him in December 2024 when he hosted the under-17 boys' and girls' teams at the Taj Pamodzi Hotel. Some progress had followed the President's directive then to restructure the debt, Mr Mweemba said, but the association remained heavily indebted. He attributed the debt to the cost of running several national teams against the income FAZ generates, and asked the government to extend its support to the junior sides when they play in COSAFA, CAF and FIFA competitions, citing an under-17 women's team that has reached three consecutive World Cups at great cost to the association.

How large the debt is depends on which line of the report is read. Mr Mweemba is quoted as saying: "The legacy debt of FAZ currently stands at not less than ZMW40 million." The article's own summary, a few paragraphs away, says the debt "stands over K140 million". The report does not reconcile the two, and no other figure was found for this edition. One of them is presumably a slip; which one cannot be established from the published account.

The President attached a condition. He said the government and the association would work together to dismantle the debt and that he had asked Mr Mweemba to write to him formally about it, describing the problem as one that "is creating problems for the development of football". But he said FAZ must manage its resources more prudently once the debt is gone, must not take on new borrowing by living beyond its means, and should spend on young players and not on consumption. He also addressed what he suggested had been an occasional rivalry between the association and the State, saying "government is never a competitor to its own FAZ" and reminding his audience that he is its patron.

The team captain, Simon Nyirenda, thanked the President for the reception and promised that the players would keep working hard, ZamFoot reported. Daily Revelation's account of the same ceremony led on a different passage, in which the President told what he called negative Zambians to turn over a new leaf and look at the good things in the country.

No date was given for the meeting with the mining houses, no sum was mentioned as a target, and the report records no reward for the players themselves. Whether the companies will be asked for sponsorship, a levy or a one-off contribution was not explained.

Debt: "not less than ZMW40 million" in Mr Mweemba's quoted words; "over K140 million" elsewhere in the same report

stories.title: Kambole in the 93rd minute: Nkana beat NAPSA Stars 1–0 in Lusaka to go top of Stream A with 16 points from seven, and ZESCO Ndola Girls win 3–0
stories.excerpt: Lazarous Kambole scored in the third minute of stoppage time at the REIZ Arena on Sunday 8 November after NAPSA goalkeeper Charles Lawu had kept Nkana out for an hour and a half, ZamFoot reported. The win puts the Kitwe side top of their stream, with no further Stream A fixtures listed until 18 November. In the women's league, ZESCO Ndola Girls beat Konkola Blades Queens 3–0 and moved to 16 points.

image.label: Kambole, 90+3
image.caption: Lazarous Kambole's stoppage-time goal gave Nkana a 1–0 win over NAPSA Stars at the REIZ Arena in Lusaka on Sunday 8 November.

body: Nkana left it as late as it can be left. Lazarous Kambole scored in the third minute of stoppage time to give the Kitwe club a 1–0 win over NAPSA Stars at the REIZ Arena in Lusaka on Sunday 8 November, a result that took them to the top of Stream A of the MTN Super League with 16 points from seven matches, ZamFoot reported on Monday.

For most of the afternoon the story was the NAPSA goalkeeper. Nkana had the early chances, Nduna Zulu shooting wide from distance in the fourth minute and heading over from a Charles Zulu free kick in the 21st, and Kambole put an effort wide in the 28th before the teams went in level. About ten minutes after the restart Nduna was through one-on-one and Charles Lawu saved; in the 67th minute Lawu saved again from Charles Zulu; shortly afterwards a Clement Mwape header from a corner went over the bar; and in the 75th Kambole, set up by Nduna, was denied by Lawu once more. The winner came at 90+3.

It was Nkana's second 1–0 win in five days, after the victory over Kansanshi Dynamos on Wednesday 4 November, and NAPSA's second 1–0 home defeat in four, after Power Dynamos beat them on Thursday 5 November, according to the results listed by BetExplorer.

No Stream A fixtures are listed before Wednesday 18 November, when Nkana go to FC MUZA, Power Dynamos host Zanaco, Konkola Blades meet Nchanga Rangers and Kansanshi Dynamos play Trident, all at 14:00, according to BetExplorer.

body.text: ZESCO Ndola Girls back to winning

body: In the Women's Super League, ZESCO Ndola Girls beat Konkola Blades Queens 3–0 at the Trade Fair Grounds in Ndola in a rescheduled Week 3 match, ZamFoot said in a report published overnight on Sunday. Thandiwe Ndhlovu scored in the 13th minute, Avell Chitundu in the 49th and Charity Mubanga in the 85th, and the win took the Ndola side to 16 points. Lesego Radiakanyo, recently signed from Gaborone United Ladies of Botswana, made her debut as a second-half substitute.

body.text: We knew we were going to face a tough opponent. We created a number of chances and missed some, but victory is important.

body: ZESCO Ndola Girls play again on Wednesday, against Trident Queens, also at the Trade Fair Grounds, the report said.

stories.title: Twenty-two for Ouagadougou: Mbewe names his under-23 squad for Burkina Faso on Wednesday, with Mandanji, Kalusa and Gift Siame in and Sabobo Banda out injured
stories.excerpt: Zambia's under-23s play Burkina Faso in Ouagadougou on Wednesday 11 November and at the National Heroes Stadium on Sunday 15 November in a two-legged qualifier for the 2027 Africa U23 Cup of Nations in Egypt, a tournament that doubles as a route to the 2028 Olympics. Coach Chisi Mbewe's squad has five players based in Egypt, Spain and the UAE. Midfielder Joseph Sabobo Banda was ruled out after an injury at his Armenian club.

image.label: Under-23s v Burkina Faso
image.caption: Zambia's under-23s meet Burkina Faso over two legs on 11 and 15 November for a place at the 2027 Africa U23 Cup of Nations.

body: Zambia's under-23 side begin their road to Egypt, and perhaps to Los Angeles, on Wednesday. Coach Chisi Mbewe has settled on a 22-man squad for the two-legged qualifier against Burkina Faso for the 2027 Africa U23 Cup of Nations, with the first leg in Ouagadougou on 11 November and the return at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka on 15 November, ZamFoot reported on Sunday 8 November. The tournament in Egypt also serves as a qualification pathway to the 2028 Olympic Games.

The squad was meant to be 23. Midfielder Joseph Sabobo Banda, who was in the provisional list, has been ruled out with an injury picked up at his club, Alashkert in Armenia, the report said, which leaves 22.

ZamFoot picked out three players. Red Arrows striker Eliya Mandanji scored in the squad's one reported preparation match, a 4–3 win over Kafue Celtic at Nkoloma Stadium. FC MUZA midfielder Given Kalusa made his senior Zambia debut in November 2025 and went on to be named in the Chipolopolo squad for the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco. Gift Siame, one of two players in the squad from the B team of the Spanish club Leganés, made his senior debut against South Africa in the same month.

Five of the 22 are listed with clubs abroad: Siame and Tumelo Mununga at Leganés B, David Simukonda at El Gouna and Pascal Phiri at Al Ittihad in Egypt, and Emmanuel Mutale at Gulf United in the United Arab Emirates. Green Eagles supply three players, more than any other club, and Kafue Celtic, Red Arrows, Kabwe Warriors and ZESCO United two each.

body: The report did not give kick-off times for either leg, say when the team was due to travel to Burkina Faso, or name the opponents the winners would face in the next round. It also gave no detail of Sabobo Banda's injury beyond the fact that it was sustained at his club.
The four days between the two legs leave little room for adjustment. Whatever happens in Ouagadougou on Wednesday, the tie will be decided in Lusaka on Sunday.

analysis.title: Botswana has answered for its government. It has not answered Khama
analysis.body: Dr Butale's statement does one thing cleanly: it tells Lusaka that a former president's words are not Gaborone's. That matters, because the remark was made in a formal chamber, by a man who once held the office, about a neighbour whose inauguration Botswana's sitting president attended. Left unanswered, it could have been read as a second channel of Botswana's foreign policy. The statement does not do the other thing critics of Mr Khama wanted, which is to rebut him. The minister defended his right to speak and said nothing, in the remarks reported, about whether the allegations are true; non-interference cuts both ways. So each side can claim something. State House can say Botswana's government has disowned the remark. Mr Khama can say nobody in authority has told him he is wrong, and that he has been neither silenced nor contradicted. What remains open is whether Zambia treats the matter as closed. Watch for any formal exchange between the two foreign ministries, for whether the Ntlo ya Dikgosi returns to the subject, and for whether the next meeting of the two countries' Bi-National Commission is used to say in public what has so far been said to newspapers.

analysis.title: 13.4% is a share, not a measure of learning, and both sides know it
analysis.body: The teachers' union and the Treasury are arguing about a ratio, and the ratio hides as much as it shows. The union's case is that a fifth of the budget is the recognised benchmark and that 13.4% falls well short. The government's case, implicit in the numbers, is that the allocation rose by more than K5 billion in a year, that school feeding is nearly doubling, and that a budget carrying K67.6 billion of debt service cannot give any sector the share it would in easier times. Both are fair. A share shrinks when the total is swollen by debt payments even if the money for classrooms grows; equally, a rising kwacha figure says nothing about what it buys once enrolment has grown under free education. The more useful question is the one News Diggers put on Monday: whether children are learning. That turns on teacher numbers, class sizes and materials, none of which the reports on the budget itemise. What to watch: the ministry's detailed estimates when they reach the parliamentary committee, how much of the K38.24 billion is salaries, and whether any published measure of learning outcomes is attached to the money.

analysis.title: Before the lunch with the mining houses, FAZ's debt needs a single number
analysis.body: A presidential promise to gather the mining companies is the most concrete offer of help the Football Association has had on its old debt, and it came with a fair condition: stop borrowing once it is cleared. But the account of the reception gives the debt as not less than K40 million in the FAZ president's quoted words and as more than K140 million a few paragraphs later. A difference of K100 million is not a rounding matter, and any company asked to contribute will want to know which it is, who is owed, and how the debt arose. There are two reasonable views of the offer itself. One is that a national association with junior teams winning abroad is a good cause for companies that earn their living in Zambia. The other is that an association's solvency should rest on its own accounts, not on appeals brokered at State House, and that corporate money raised this way can come with expectations. What to watch: FAZ's formal letter to the President, whether audited figures for the debt are published, and whether the meeting with the mining houses is given a date.
